paras: The killing of Eugene Burke was the fatal shooting of Eugene Burke (also spelled Burk), a Black hotel worker, by a white pursuer after a crowd chased him from near the Kingan packing plant in Indianapolis, Indiana, on June 9, 1903. Burke had been accused of insulting a thirteen-year-old white girl, and the man who fired, Meade Barr, was later convicted of manslaughter. Editors North and South called it a lynching.

Burke worked as a porter or waiter at the English Hotel and was 22, according to one wire report. Gertrude Worth, thirteen, was gathering kindling wood around the packing plant when Burke approached her, the Indianapolis Journal reported. Barr, a 25-year-old former soldier who had served in the Philippines, worked at Kingan's under the name James Anderson.

According to the Journal, Burke grabbed the girl by the arm and "grossly" insulted her, and her cries drew men and boys from the neighborhood. The New York Sun's dispatch said only that he was seen to talk to her, and that Kingan employees who had watched him began the chase when he walked away.

The pursuit crossed the I., D. & W. railroad bridge "with the angry mob howling close on his heels," in the Journal's words, and the Sun put the crowd at 200. Some pursuers turned back after the bridge, but Barr kept on and fired a revolver as Burke turned and threw a stone at him, the Journal said. Shot in the abdomen, Burke fell over an embankment and died at City Hospital about an hour later, while the shooter slipped away through the railroad yards.

Police traced Barr to Elizabethtown, and City Detective Chauncy A. Manning brought him back to Indianapolis by June 12. Questioned at the police station, Barr said, "Sure, I killed him," and that he had intended to kill Burke when he started after him.

On June 17 Worth testified at the coroner's office that Burke had grabbed her arm and tried to lure her away. She also said that Cecil Horton had urged her to go with Burke so that "the gang of boys would follow them and fix the colored man," and Horton was jailed as Barr's accomplice.

The Marion County grand jury indicted Barr for murder on July 14. At his September trial the defense argued self-defense, and on September 22 the jury found him guilty of manslaughter; he was fined $1 and sentenced to two to twenty-one years in the Indiana Reformatory.

The Indianapolis Journal followed the case to the sentence, headlining its first report "A MOB PURSUED THE NEGRO" and treating the insult as established. It printed Barr's boasts at length, and answering a New York Sun letter on Northern race prejudice, it called such incidents "unimportant."
Wire briefs ran under headlines such as "NEGRO SPOKE TO A GIRL," and a later dispatch in the Ocala Evening Star, headed with a slur, called the shooter "A Negro Ex-Soldier."

Northern editors called it a lynching: the Daily Kennebec Journal termed it "about the worst lynching outrage of the season," with no crime, no complaint and no arrests. A Newark Advertiser editorial, reprinted in the Evening Journal and the Americus Times-Recorder, said a Southern mob "never did worse," and the Springfield Republican said the girl's testimony should have been taken first.

Southern papers turned it against Northern critics: the Savannah Morning News found race prejudice as strong in Indianapolis as in Tangipahoa parish, and the Free Lance, quoted in the Virginia Citizen, said no Southern place would take "such a supposition" as "a pretext to take human life."
No Black-press report of the killing was found; the Indianapolis Freeman's column that week took up lynch law and local race incidents without naming Burke.

Accounts of Burke's conduct ranged from a "supposed insulting remark" in the first wire to a grab at the girl's arm in the Journal and an attempted stabbing in Barr's statement. Barr's counsel said Burke reached for a revolver, the Journal's first report that he threw a stone, and Northern editorials that he was shot in the back. The Sun gave a mob of 200, but the Journal and Barr said most pursuers had dropped out before the shot.

bases: A crowd of Kingan employees and bystanders chased Burke after he was accused of insulting a white girl, and one pursuer shot him dead; editors North and South called it a lynching (A1, A2, A9).

Burke was killed without legal authority after a crowd put at 200 chased him for an alleged insult to a white girl (A1, A2), but the local paper and the shooter say the other pursuers dropped out before one man fired, and a jury convicted that man of manslaughter (A1, A6, A26).
The Indianapolis Journal's local report and independent wire versions agree on the chase and fatal shooting near Kingan's, and the shooter admitted it and was convicted (A1, A2, A6, A26).

accounts.gist: Burke stopped on the Big Four bridge and reached for a revolver, and Barr fired first in self-defense.

accounts.label: Northern editors
accounts.gist: A Black man seen speaking to a white girl was chased by a mob and shot in the back with no crime or complaint and no arrests.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal headlined 'A MOB PURSUED THE NEGRO' and treated the insult as fact, printed Barr's boasts, then covered his prosecution to conviction and editorially called the incident 'unimportant'.
Northern editors (Kennebec Journal, Newark Advertiser, Springfield Republican) called it a lynching for no crime and evidence that lynching was not only Southern.

Southern papers used the case against Northern critics; the Savannah Morning News blamed Burk's 'familiarity with white women', while the Free Lance said no Southern place would kill on 'such a supposition'.
Wire briefs ran under headlines such as 'NEGRO SPOKE TO A GIRL', 'COLORED MAN SHOT' and the slur 'A CHIVALROUS 'COON'.
The Indianapolis Freeman column that week criticized lynch law and local race incidents but did not name Burke.
